title: Show HN: Euspell – Spelling reform: an enginnering approach

item.text:
Hi HN. Euspell is a conservastive respelling of English and all the software needed to implement it. The link above converts the text you paste, in your browser. Other ways to try it out are the browser extensions and EPUB/PDF readers.

Previous spelling reforms have failed for two reasons: they asked people to apply rules by hand or remember a large set of new spellings, and they couldn't handle homographs: "read" is reed or red, "records" is a noun or a verb, "wound" is an injury or a past tense - writing in pure phonetics will actually create hundreds of homographs. Euspell approaches spelling reform differently, with the goal of aiding reading and comprehension.

- A lexicon with 205505 entries, each with CLAWS7 part-of-speech tags. Of these, 164067 (80%) are left unchanged. No diacritics are used. Proper nouns are untouched. American spelling is the base, in the line of Webster's reforms. - 5920 entries are ambiguous and need context. The noun/verb -s split (records/recordz) is a linear SVM: 93.2% on held-out text. The hand-written rule it replaced scored 75.9%. The full evaluation is at https://github.com/ossiak/euspell/blob/main/docs/paper-evalu... - Semantic splits (e.g. bow, tear, lead) are hand-written rules and less accurate: "read" gets about four in five right on its test set. - Runs locally in a browser extension (Chrome/Firefox/Safari, including PDFs), MS Word, LibreOffice, Google Docs, and a standalone EPUB/PDF reader for Windows, MacOS, Android and iOS. - Code is GPL-3.0, lexicon is CC BY-SA 4.0: https://github.com/ossiak/euspell. White paper: https://euspell.org/paper

The changes can be toggled on and off: Euspell changes what you read, not the source text. AI tools (Claude) helped with the software, the site and the videos; the reform and the lexicon are mine. There is also a 14-part video series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLfCd5hTV7IWg

Most useful feedback: sentences where it picks the wrong spelling.

sources.text:
Try it
Read your own text in euspell
Paste any English text. It is converted in your browser, by the same engine the extension runs, and nothing you type leaves this page.
Examples
Homographs
Silent letters
Plain prose
Clear
Traditional spelling
She records every meeting and keeps the records in a drawer. I wound the bandage around the wound. I want to read the book she read last year. The wind was too strong to wind the sail. She shed a tear when she saw the tear in her coat.
Euspell
Loading the lexicon: about 1.7 MB, once.
Mark the changed words (hover one for its old spelling)
Copy euspell
What you are looking at
Each word is looked up in the lexicon, and most are left exactly as they are. The ones that change are marked. A word like
records
,
wound
or
read
has two pronunciations and so two euspellings, and which one it gets depends on
what it is doing in the sentence
: the engine tags the words around it before choosing.
It gets most of those right, not all of them. If a word comes out wrong,
tell us which one and in what sentence
. That is the most useful report there is.
The page downloads the engine and the lexicon once, about 1.7 MB between them, and converts everything locally. There is no server behind it to send text to.

comments.text:
ok; I'll be that person: enginnering <~ engineering
conservastive <~ conservative Normally, i just don't care about a person's spelling.  In fact, in these days of LLM tokenized prose, a little random keyboard 'mahsup' can be endearing.  However, proposing a spelling help product that was made with an LLM, and then either aren't using it or it doesn't work.  Not a strong Show HN outing. I like the semantic approach though. Using context to identify the words which are likely and checking those for correct spelling is novel, at least to my awareness.  Perhaps look for options to 'de-Webster' the spelling as an user choice.  The American version of English is not automatically the best in all cases, much like the Oxford comma rule is not always the right way to compose a long list of similar ideas within the same sentence. Colourful and creative authors prefer to have freedom, to choose how they organise the spelling, prose, structure and composition of their verse.
